name: Carlos Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the Dry Creek depot, mostly on rural line upgrades and hooking up the new solar farms that keep popping up on old farmland. So one week we're rebuilding a sagging line along a country road, the next we're building the connection from a solar farm into the network. I like the solar work, it's new and every site is different, and the developers pay attention to you because you're holding up their money. What wears me out is the heat in summer, out in an open field with no shade, in full flame-resistant gear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home, and how you see the job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Lucia is the accountant at a dental clinic in town, and we've got Mateo, who's thirteen, and Ines, who's ten. Mortgage on a house with a big shed out back, which is my workshop, and about three months of savings. I use AI every day: I plan jobs with it, I've had it teach me about solar inverters, I even used it to draft a business plan for a contracting company I'd like to start one day. My father ran a small hardware store, so I grew up thinking you should build something of your own. We go to Mass most weeks, and I coach Mateo's basketball team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, the hype was overblown, but the tools are still good if you know how to use them. I'd probably post that the people who learned them will still be ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plan stays on track. The solar farms keep coming, the rural lines keep needing upgrades, and I keep using AI to work smarter. I'd still want to start my own contracting company in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep learning, keep saving toward the business. Maybe take on some private jobs on weekends, connecting farm sheds and small solar setups, to build a customer list. Keep the mortgage ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit impatient to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the contracting company you'd like to start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small outfit doing the connections for solar farms and farm buildings out here, where the big contractors don't like to drive. Two trucks, four or five guys. I've got the business plan on my laptop, the AI helped me with the cash flow, and Lucia checked the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Lucia say when she checked them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She said the plan was good but the savings weren't. She wants six months of the family's costs in the bank before I quit the company. Fair enough, she's the accountant.

S0.say: The hype was overblown, but the tools are still good if you know how to use them. The people who learned them will still be ahead.
S0.think: His plan stays on track: solar farms keep coming, rural lines need upgrades and he keeps using AI to work smarter. He still wants to start his own contracting company in a few years.
S0.do: Keeps working out of the Dry Creek depot, learning and saving toward the business. Takes private weekend jobs connecting farm sheds and small solar setups to build a customer list.
S0.feel: Calm, and a bit impatient to get on with it.
S0.quote: She said the plan was good but the savings weren't.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos is an entrepreneur in waiting who uses AI daily as a learning tool. His wife is the financial brake on his ambitions, and he respects it. His drive to build something of his own comes from his father's store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people willing to work. The market will reward people who learn fast and take a bit of risk. I wouldn't want the government getting in the way, but I'd want good apprenticeships for young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it helps my plan. If AI can do the design and paperwork for solar connections, a small company like mine can compete with the big ones. Fewer people in the office, more time in the field. That's exactly what I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the business plan forward by a year. Learn every tool the company brings in, and some they don't. Do more weekend jobs to build savings to six months, like Lucia wants. Maybe buy a used bucket truck once the savings are there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited actually. A bit nervous about the money side, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a used bucket truck. What would that cost, and where would it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decent used one is maybe forty thousand. I'd want to put a quarter down from savings and finance the rest against the first contracts. Lucia would want to see signed contracts before I signed anything. She's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older guys who don't want to learn. I'd offer them work in my company if they were good on the tools, but I'd need them to use the software. I can't carry people, it's a small business.

S1.say: This is a chance for people willing to work, and the market will reward those who learn fast and take risks. He'd keep government out of the way but wants good apprenticeships for young people.
S1.think: It helps his plan, because AI doing design and paperwork lets a small company compete with the big ones. Fewer people in the office and more time in the field is what he wants.
S1.do: Brings the business plan forward by a year and learns every new tool. Builds savings to six months through weekend jobs and plans to buy a used bucket truck, about forty thousand, with a quarter down once contracts are signed.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, with a little nervousness about money.
S1.quote: I can't carry people, it's a small business.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks to him like the perfect opening for his business. He's frank that he wouldn't keep colleagues who won't adapt. His plans stay tied to his wife's conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to take responsibility and move fast, not wait for someone to save them. Families and churches should help each other. I'd be wary of the government trying to control it, they'd make it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years would shake me. If robots can do the connections, then my company has no work, or it's just me and a couple of robots, if I can even afford them. The big firms would buy fleets and undercut me. Three months of savings doesn't fight that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on starting the company, no point buying a truck that a robot makes worthless. I'd save hard and cut the extras, the new kitchen Lucia wanted waits. I'd look at whether I could become a dealer or installer for the robots themselves, selling to farms and small utilities. That's the only angle I'd see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel I had some moves, but the board would be a lot smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mateo and Ines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the world's changing and their dad's going to find a way, like their grandpa did when the big hardware chain came to town. He lost the store but he started a repair business out of the garage. I'd tell them that story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' notice, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn everything about the robots, who makes them, how they're serviced, what they cost. If I can't beat them, I'd want to be the guy who sells and fixes them out here. And pray, honestly. Lucia and I would pray on it.

S2.say: People need to take responsibility and move fast rather than wait to be saved. Families and churches should help each other, and government control would make it worse.
S2.think: Two years would shake him: robots doing the connections would leave his company with no work, and big firms with robot fleets would undercut him. Three months of savings can't fight that.
S2.do: Holds off on starting the company and saves hard, delaying the new kitchen. Learns everything about the robots and looks at becoming a dealer and service installer for them on farms and at small utilities.
S2.feel: Anxious, with some moves left but a much smaller board.
S2.quote: I'd tell them the world's changing and their dad's going to find a way, like their grandpa did when the big hardware chain came to town.
S2.fieldNote: Even the fast scenario sends him looking for an angle rather than shelter. His father's story of losing a store and starting over anchors him. Faith and family are his support, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work. Start now, learn the new tools, and don't count on a handout. I'd say it at the basketball club and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is tight but workable. I could start the company in a year, run it for three or four, and then turn it into a business that uses robots instead of competing with them. I'd be 48, with something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the company next year with one truck and two guys. Buy robot equipment as soon as it's affordable, maybe 2029 or 2030, and get trained to run and service it. Save hard in the meantime. Lucia keeps her job, so we have one steady income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. It feels like a bet I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying robots for your own company. Isn't that putting people out of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I've thought about it. If I don't, someone bigger will, and then nobody local has a job at all. I'd rather it was me, here, keeping some guys on to run and fix them. That's how I'd see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between starting a business and abandoning one. With two years, the truck's worthless before it's paid off. With five, I can earn it back and then switch to robots. Timing is everything for a small business.

S3.say: Five years is enough for anyone willing to work: start now, learn the new tools and don't count on a handout. He'd say it at the basketball club and online.
S3.think: Five years is tight but workable: he could start the company, run it for a few years, then switch to using robots instead of competing with them. At 48 he'd have something of his own.
S3.do: Starts the company next year with one truck and two workers, and buys robot equipment once affordable, around 2029 or 2030, training to run and service it. Saves hard while Lucia's job provides a steady income.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like a bet he could win.
S3.quote: It's the difference between starting a business and abandoning one.
S3.fieldNote: Carlos sees timing as decisive and treats five years as enough to build and then convert his business. He faced the question of putting people out of work directly and justified it as keeping local jobs. His wife's steady income is his safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone with a bit of drive. Build something, learn the new tools, and teach your kids to do the same. Less talk about what government should do, more about what we can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the best case for me. I'd build the company, grow it, and bring in robots when they're proven, not first. By 2036 I'd want to own a business that runs robot crews across this whole region, with a few good people overseeing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the company in a year, grow to two or three trucks by 2030, invest in robots around 2032. Put some profit into a pension and some into land, because land always matters. Help Mateo and Ines see that owning something is safer than working for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Excited. Ten years is enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy robots when they're proven, not first. That sounds cautious for you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, Lucia's rubbing off on me. With ten years you don't need to be first, you need to be right. Let the big firms pay for the early mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your kids to take from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That work matters and so does owning what you work with. My father had the store, I'd have the company, and maybe Mateo takes it on. Ines says she wants to be a lawyer, which with robots might be a bad bet, but she's ten, she'll change her mind.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift for anyone with drive: build something, learn the tools and teach your kids the same. There should be less talk about government and more about what people can do.
S4.think: Ten years is his best case: build and grow the company, bring in robots once proven and by 2036 own a business running robot crews across the region with a few people overseeing them.
S4.do: Starts the company within a year, grows to two or three trucks by 2030 and invests in robots around 2032. Puts profit into a pension and land, and teaches his kids that owning something is safer than working for someone.
S4.feel: Calm and excited, sure ten years is enough to build something.
S4.quote: With ten years you don't need to be first, you need to be right.
S4.fieldNote: The long runway turns AGI into an opportunity in his eyes. He has absorbed some of his wife's caution about timing. He hopes to pass the business on, echoing his father's store.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it kills the business before it starts. What would help is time, honestly, and fair rules so small companies can buy robots too, not just the giants. Maybe cheap loans for small businesses to switch over. And apprenticeships, so young people learn how the robots work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the robots. If it's three big companies, we're all just renting our lives from them. If it's lots of small local firms, then people like me still have a stake.

headlineQuote: If it's three big companies, we're all just renting our lives from them.
portrait: Carlos Silva is a 43-year-old lineworker who upgrades rural lines and connects new solar farms, uses AI every day and has a business plan on his laptop for his own contracting company. His wife Lucia, an accountant, keeps his ambitions in check, and they have two kids, a mortgage and about three months saved. A son of a hardware store owner, he believes in self-reliance, faith and owning what you work with. Steady change looks like a perfect opening, and fast AGI shakes him because it would kill the business before it starts, but with five or ten years he plans to build the company and then run it with robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would kill his contracting business before it could start.
whatWouldHelp: More time, fair rules so small firms can buy robots and not just the giants, cheap loans for small businesses to switch over, and apprenticeships teaching young people how robots work.
